:::{#exm-aic-bic-compare}
#### Comparing two models by AIC and BIC

Suppose two candidate models are fit to the same $n = 100$ observations.
Model A has $p = 3$ parameters
and maximized log-likelihood $\est{\llik}_A = -120.0$,
while model B has $p = 5$ parameters and $\est{\llik}_B = -118.5$.
Then

$$
\ba
\text{AIC}_A
&= -2(-120.0) + 2 \cdot 3
&& \text{(AIC formula)} \\
&= 240 + 6
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= 246
&& \text{(add)} \\
\text{AIC}_B
&= -2(-118.5) + 2 \cdot 5
&& \text{(AIC formula)} \\
&= 237 + 10
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= 247
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

and, with $\logf{100} \approx 4.605$,

$$
\ba
\text{BIC}_A
&= 240 + 3 \logf{100}
&& \text{(BIC formula)} \\
&\approx 240 + 13.82
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= 253.82
&& \text{(add)} \\
\text{BIC}_B
&= 237 + 5 \logf{100}
&& \text{(BIC formula)} \\
&\approx 237 + 23.03
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= 260.03
&& \text{(add)}
\ea
$$

Both criteria prefer model A.
Model B fits better ($\est{\llik}_B > \est{\llik}_A$),
but the penalty for its two extra parameters is larger than the gain from that better fit.
The AIC difference is only 1,
which is negligible,
while the BIC difference of about 6.2 favors model A more clearly,
because BIC charges $\logf{100} \approx 4.6$ per parameter instead of 2.

:::
